This project examines the relationship between the U.S. stock market and the 10-year U.S. Treasury yield from 2000 through 2026. The S&P 500 is used to represent stock-market performance, while the 10-year Treasury yield represents conditions in the U.S. bond market. Historical S&P 500 data were obtained through Yahoo Finance, while Treasury yield data were collected from the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis Federal Reserve Economic Data (FRED). Using R, I analyze the relationship between daily S&P 500 returns and changes in the 10-year Treasury yield, with particular attention to how this relationship changed during the 2008–2009 Financial Crisis and the 2020 COVID-19 market shock.

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
source(file.path(Sys.getenv("QUARTO_PROJECT_DIR", "../.."), "R/theme_isai.R"))
use_isai_defaults()
```

```{r}
#| label: Loaded Data
#| include: false
library(quantmod)
library(fredr)
library(tidyverse)
fredr_has_key()

getSymbols(
  "^GSPC",
  src= "yahoo",
  from = "2000-01-01",
  to = "2026-08-20"
)

sp500 <- data.frame(
  date = index(GSPC), 
  sp500 = as.numeric(Cl(GSPC))
)

treasury10 <- fredr(
  series_id = "DGS10",
  observation_start = as.Date("2000-01-01")
)|>
  select(date, value)|>
  rename(treasury10 = value)


stock_bond <- sp500|>
  inner_join(treasury10, by = "date")

range(sp500$date)
range(treasury10$date)
range(stock_bond$date)

```

```{r}
#| label: Change/Return
#| include: false
library(quantmod)
library(fredr)
library(tidyverse)

stock_bond <- stock_bond |>
  arrange(date) |>
  mutate(
    sp500_return = (sp500 / lag(sp500)) - 1,
    treasury10_change = treasury10 - lag(treasury10)
  )

head(stock_bond)
```

```{r}
#| label: CleanStockBond
#| include: false
library(quantmod)
library(fredr)
library(tidyverse)

stock_bond_clean <- stock_bond |>
  drop_na(sp500_return, treasury10_change)

summary(stock_bond_clean)
```

```{r}
#| label: SP500&10TGraph
#| fig-alt: !expr c("Line chart of the S&P 500 index from 2000 to 2026. It falls in the early 2000s and again in 2008 to 2009, then climbs steadily, most steeply after 2020.", "Line chart of the 10-year U.S. Treasury yield from 2000 to 2026. It falls from about 6 percent to below 1 percent in 2020, then rises to around 4 to 5 percent after 2022.")
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| column: page
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 4
#| echo: false
library(quantmod)
library(fredr)
library(tidyverse)

ggplot(stock_bond, aes(x = date, y = sp500)) +
  geom_line() + 
  labs(
    title = "S&P 500 Performance, 2000-2026",
    x = "Year",
    y = "S&P 500"
  )

ggplot(stock_bond, aes(x = date, y = treasury10)) +
  geom_line() + 
  labs(
    title = "10-Year U.S. Treasury Yield, 2000-2026",
    x = "Year",
    y = "10-Year Treasury Yield(%)"
  )
```

::: panel-tabset
## Chart

```{r}
#| label: Scatterplot
#| fig-alt: "Scatterplot of daily S&P 500 returns against daily changes in the 10-year Treasury yield, 2000 to 2026: a dense cloud of points centered on zero with an upward-sloping regression line."
#| message: false
#| echo: false
library(quantmod)
library(fredr)
library(tidyverse)

ggplot(
  stock_bond_clean,
  aes(
    x = treasury10_change,
    y = sp500_return
  )
) + 
  geom_point(alpha = 0.25) + 
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") + 
  labs(
    title = "S&P 500 Returns vs. 10-Year Treasury Yield Changes",
    x = "Change in 10-Year Treasury Yield",
    y = "S&P 500 Daily Return"
  )
```

## Regression output

```{r}
#| label: Line Regression
library(quantmod)
library(fredr)
library(tidyverse)

model1 <- lm(
  sp500_return ~ treasury10_change, 
  data = stock_bond_clean
)

summary(model1)
```
:::

::: finding
A linear regression of daily S&P 500 returns on daily changes in the 10-year Treasury yield from 2000–2026 found a statistically significant positive association (β = 0.060, p \< 0.001). However, the model's R² of 0.082 indicates that Treasury yield changes alone explain only a small portion of daily equity-return variation.
:::

## How did the relationship between U.S. stock-market returns and changes in 10-year Treasury yields differ between the 2008–2009 financial crisis and the 2020 COVID-19 market shock?

```{r}
#| label: FinancialC_dataDate
#| include: false
library(quantmod)
library(fredr)
library(tidyverse)

financial_crisis <- stock_bond_clean |>
  filter(
    date >= as.Date("2008-01-01"),
    date <= as.Date("2009-12-31")
  )

range(financial_crisis$date)
```

```{r}
#| label: covid_dataDate
#| include: false
covid <- stock_bond_clean |>
  filter(
    date >= as.Date("2020-01-01"),
    date <= as.Date("2020-12-31")
  )

range(covid$date)
```

```{r}
#| label: Correlation
#| include: false
financial_crisis_clean <- financial_crisis |>
  drop_na(sp500_return, treasury10_change)

cor(
  financial_crisis_clean$sp500_return,
  financial_crisis_clean$treasury10_change
)

covid_clean <- covid |>
  drop_na(sp500_return, treasury10_change)

cor(
  covid_clean$sp500_return,
  covid_clean$treasury10_change
)
```

::: {.column-page layout-ncol="2"}
```{r}
#| label: FinC_graph
#| fig-alt: "Scatterplot of daily S&P 500 returns against daily 10-year Treasury yield changes during the 2008 to 2009 financial crisis, with an upward-sloping regression line."
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 4.2
#| message: false
#| echo: false
ggplot(
  financial_crisis_clean,
  aes(
    x= treasury10_change,
    y=sp500_return
  )
) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) + 
  geom_smooth(method = "lm")+
  labs(
    title = "S&P500 returns vs. Treasury Yields Changes",
    subtitle = "2008-2009 Financial Crisis",
    x = "Change in 10-Year Treasury Yield",
    y = "S&P 500 Daily Return"
  )
```

```{r}
#| label: CovidGraph
#| fig-alt: "Scatterplot of daily S&P 500 returns against daily 10-year Treasury yield changes during 2020, with a steeper upward-sloping regression line."
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 4.2
#| message: false
#| echo: false
ggplot(
  covid_clean,
  aes(
    x=treasury10_change,
    y=sp500_return
  )
) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) + 
  geom_smooth(method = "lm")+
  labs(
    title = "S&P500 returns vs. Treasury Yields Changes",
    subtitle = "Covid-19 2020 Period",
    x = "Change in 10-Year Treasury Yield",
    y = "S&P 500 Daily Return"
  )
```
:::

::: panel-tabset
## 2008–2009 model

```{r}
#| label: financialc_model
#| echo: false
financial_model <- lm(
  sp500_return ~ treasury10_change,
  data = financial_crisis
)

summary(financial_model)
```

## 2020 model

```{r}
#| label: covid_model
#| echo: false
covid_model <- lm(
  sp500_return ~ treasury10_change,
  data = covid
)

summary(covid_model)
```
:::

```{r}
#| label: Comparison
#| include: false
comparison <- data.frame(
  Period = c(
    "2000–2026",
    "2008-2009 Financial Crisis",
    "2020 COVID-19"
  ),
  
  Correlation = c(
    cor(
      stock_bond_clean$sp500_return,
      stock_bond_clean$treasury10_change
    ),
    
    cor(
      financial_crisis_clean$sp500_return,
      financial_crisis_clean$treasury10_change
    ),
    
    cor(
      covid_clean$sp500_return,
      covid_clean$treasury10_change
    )
  ),
  
  Beta = c(
    coef(model1)["treasury10_change"],
    coef(financial_model)["treasury10_change"],
    coef(covid_model)["treasury10_change"]
  ),
  
  R_squared = c(
    summary(model1)$r.squared,
    summary(financial_model)$r.squared,
    summary(covid_model)$r.squared
  )
)

comparison
```

::: finding
The relationship between S&P 500 returns and changes in 10-year Treasury yields strengthened during periods of major financial stress. This is reflected in the increase in R² from 0.082 during 2000–2026 to 0.1495 during the 2008–2009 Financial Crisis and 0.2303 during the 2020 COVID-19 period. Thus, changes in Treasury yields explained a greater proportion of the variation in daily S&P 500 returns during both crises.
:::

```{r}
#| label: Crisis_stats
#| include: false
crisis_stats_long <- comparison |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(Correlation, Beta, R_squared),
    names_to = "Statistics", 
    values_to = "Value"
  )|>
  mutate(
    Value = if_else(
      Statistics == "R_squared",
      Value * 100,
      Value
    )
  )

crisis_stats_long <- crisis_stats_long |>
  mutate(
    Statistics = recode(
      Statistics,
      "Correlation" = "Correlation",
      "Beta" = "Regression Beta",
      "R_squared" = "R² (%)"
    )
  )

crisis_stats_long
```

```{r}
#| label: Stats Bar
#| fig-alt: "Three bar charts comparing 2000 to 2026, the 2008 to 2009 financial crisis, and 2020 on correlation, R-squared in percent, and regression beta. All three measures rise from the full period to the 2008 to 2009 crisis to 2020."
#| column: page
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4.6
#| echo: false
ggplot(
  crisis_stats_long,
  aes(x = Period, y = Value)
) + 
  geom_col() + 
  facet_wrap(~ Statistics, scales = "free_y") + 
  labs(
    title = "Stock-Treasury Relationship During Major Crises",
    subtitle = "Comparison of correlation, regression coefficient, and R²",
    x = "Period/Crisis",
    y = "Value"
  ) + 
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)
  )
```

## What changed after 2022?

The crisis models treat each period as a separate window. To see how the relationship moved over time, I calculated the correlation between daily S&P 500 returns and daily changes in the 10-year Treasury yield over a rolling window of the previous 250 trading days, about one year.

```{r}
#| label: Rolling_corr
#| include: false
library(zoo)

rolling <- stock_bond_clean |>
  arrange(date)

rolling$roll_cor <- rollapplyr(
  seq_len(nrow(rolling)),
  250,
  function(i) cor(rolling$sp500_return[i], rolling$treasury10_change[i]),
  fill = NA
)

rolling <- rolling |>
  drop_na(roll_cor)

before_2022 <- rolling |>
  filter(date < as.Date("2022-01-01"))

since_2022 <- rolling |>
  filter(date >= as.Date("2022-01-01"))

lowest <- since_2022 |>
  slice_min(roll_cor, n = 1)
```

```{r}
#| label: Rolling_graph
#| echo: false
#| column: page
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4.2
#| fig-alt: "Line chart of the rolling one-year correlation between daily S&P 500 returns and daily 10-year Treasury yield changes, 2001 to 2026. It stays mostly between 0.2 and 0.6, with shaded bands for the 2008 to 2009 crisis and 2020, then drops below zero for most of the period after 2022."
periods <- tibble(
  start = as.Date(c("2008-01-01", "2020-01-01", "2022-01-01")),
  end   = as.Date(c("2009-12-31", "2020-12-31", as.character(max(rolling$date)))),
  label = c("2008–09\nfinancial crisis", "COVID-19\nshock", "Since 2022"),
  fill  = c("crisis", "crisis", "recent")
)

ggplot(rolling, aes(x = date, y = roll_cor)) +
  geom_rect(
    data = periods,
    aes(xmin = start, xmax = end, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = fill),
    inherit.aes = FALSE
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(crisis = isai_pal[["shock"]], recent = "#F3E7D3"),
    guide = "none"
  ) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = isai_pal[["ink"]], linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_line(colour = isai_pal[["equities"]], linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_text(
    data = periods,
    aes(x = start + (end - start) / 2, y = 0.85, label = label),
    inherit.aes = FALSE, size = 3.2, colour = "#5A6672", lineheight = 0.95
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(-0.45, 0.95), breaks = seq(-0.4, 0.8, 0.4)) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "5 years", date_labels = "%Y") +
  labs(
    title = "Rolling One-Year Correlation: S&P 500 Returns vs. 10-Year Treasury Yield Changes",
    subtitle = "250-trading-day window",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Correlation"
  )
```

::: finding
From `r format(min(before_2022$date), "%Y")` through 2021, the rolling correlation averaged `r sprintf("%.2f", mean(before_2022$roll_cor))` and was positive on `r round(100 * mean(before_2022$roll_cor > 0))`% of trading days: stocks tended to rise on days when Treasury yields rose. Since 2022, a period that began as the Federal Reserve started raising interest rates, that pattern has broken down. The correlation averaged `r sprintf("%.2f", mean(since_2022$roll_cor))`, was negative on `r round(100 * mean(since_2022$roll_cor < 0))`% of trading days, and reached `r sprintf("%.2f", lowest$roll_cor)` in `r format(lowest$date, "%B %Y")`. In the most recent period, rising yields have more often coincided with falling stock prices, the opposite of the pattern that held for the previous two decades. Like the regressions above, this measures association, not cause.
:::
